paper.title: Inequality of Opportunity for Income in Denmark and the United States: A Comparison Based on Administrative Data
paper.journal: NBER Working Paper Series, Working Paper 27835

registers.role: outcomes (own income), treatment (gender and parental income), sample frame

registers.name_in_paper: Statistics of Income Mobility (SOI-M) Panel (Mitnik et al. 2015)
registers.years: built from U.S. tax returns, W-2 forms and other administrative sources; incomes used for 2010
registers.role: U.S. outcomes, treatment and sample frame

registers.name_in_paper: Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), 'Sample I' from Mitnik (2019)
registers.role: lifecycle-bias adjustment factors for overall income inequality

registers.name_in_paper: Annual Social and Economic Supplement of the 2011 Current Population Survey (CPS-ASEC)
registers.role: adjustment factors for U.S. disposable income (state taxes and omitted transfers)

registers.name_in_paper: publicly available aggregate tax-based U.S. statistics from Chetty et al. (2020b), the Opportunity Atlas
registers.role: adjustment factors for race and ethnicity in the U.S. extension
variables_mentioned: income rank by gender, parental income percentile bin and race/ethnicity

linkages: People are linked to their parents; the Danish sample replicates as much as possible the approach used in the SOI-M Panel to assign parents to people and to define families (Mitnik et al. 2015:16-19)
Parental income is the average disposable family income of the parents over the years when the person was 15-23 years old

sample.universe: People born 1972-1975 who were 35-38 years old in 2010: in Denmark, the full resident population covered by the administrative registers; in the United States, all people born 1972-1975 living in the U.S. in 1987, as represented by the SOI-M Panel
selection_rules: Exclude people with more than 3 years of missing parental information
Exclude people with nonpositive average parental income
In analyses where total or disposable income is the outcome, exclude people with negative total or disposable income
The Danish sample also excludes those not living in Denmark in 1987 (to match the population represented by the SOI-M Panel)
sample.period: 2010 (own income); parental income averaged over the years when the person was 15-23 years old
sample.n_observations: Denmark: 262,201 (income analyses) and 263,254 (earnings analyses); United States: 12,805 (income analyses) and 13,107 (earnings analyses)

construction_notes: 100 types are defined by crossing gender with fiftiles (50 groups of 2 percent) of average parental disposable income; gender-specific analyses use 50 types defined by parental income fiftile alone
Inequality of opportunity is computed nonparametrically (Checchi-Peragine): within-type means are assigned to individuals and an inequality index is computed over the resulting distribution

Earnings include 65 percent of self-employment income in both countries (the other 35 percent treated as return to capital); Danish total income includes 100 percent of self-employment income, capital income and unemployment insurance
Total (disposable) income per adult equals total (disposable) income for single people and half of it for married people

U.S. disposable income subtracts net federal taxes including refundable credits; state taxes and some transfers are not excised, and ex-post adjustment factors from the CPS-ASEC are applied in Table 6
All income variables are expressed in 2010 dollars using the Danish CPI and the U.S. CPI-U-RS; Danish kroner are converted at a PPP exchange rate of 758.6 kroner per 100 dollars
Estimates of overall income inequality are divided by lifecycle-bias adjustment factors computed from the PSID: 1.11 (Gini), 1.22 (Kakwani), 1.12 (Piesch), 1.10 (Mehran), 1.11 (RMD)
U.S. estimates use SOI-M Panel sampling weights; income and marital status of nonfilers are multiply imputed within the bootstrap

Inference: nonparametric bootstrap with 2,000 repetitions; bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals for point and lower-bound estimates; Imbens and Manski (2004) confidence intervals for partially identified quantities

claims.statement: Lower-bound absolute inequality of opportunity for individual earnings (Gini coefficient) in Denmark, men and women pooled, is 0.118.

treatment.label: Circumstances beyond people's control: gender and fiftile of parental income

definition.value: Types are defined by crossing gender with fiftiles of average parental disposable income (fiftiles are like quintiles but each contains 2 percent of the population), giving 100 types; for estimates produced separately for men and women, types are defined by parental income fiftile alone. Parental income is the average disposable family income of the person's parents when the person was 15-23 years old.

timing.value: Gender is fixed at birth; parental disposable income is averaged over the years in which the person was 15-23 years old (roughly 1987-1998 for these cohorts).

outcome.label: Individual earnings

definition.value: Individual labour earnings measured in 2010. In the U.S. data, the sum of W-2 wages and 65 percent of self-employment income when positive (the other 35 percent is assumed to be the return to capital); in the Danish data, earnings likewise include 65 percent of self-employment income. All income variables are expressed in 2010 U.S. dollars (CPI deflators; Danish kroner converted at a PPP rate of 758.6 kroner per 100 dollars).

timing.value: Measured in 2010, when the people in the sample were 35-38 years old; the quantity of interest is long-run income, for which the 2010 measure is a proxy.

units.value: Gini coefficient of within-type mean individual earnings (unitless, 0-1)

magnitude.interpretation: Gini coefficient of the distribution of within-type mean individual earnings; a lower bound for absolute inequality of opportunity because only gender and parental income rank define types.

estimand.target_population: People born 1972-1975, aged 35-38 in 2010, in Denmark
estimand.time_horizon: Income measured in 2010, when the people in the sample were 35-38 years old
estimand.formal_query: D(E(Y|C)) with D = Gini, C = (gender, parental income fiftile), Y = individual earnings

population.description: People born 1972-1975 who were 35-38 years old in 2010 in Denmark. Administrative register data covering the full Danish population.
population.period: 2010 (own income); parental income averaged over the years in which the person was 15-23 years old
subgroups_defined: gender
fiftiles of average parental disposable income
race and ethnicity (U.S. extension only, via Chetty et al. 2020b aggregates)
population.selection: Excludes people with more than 3 years of missing parental information and with nonpositive average parental income; income analyses also exclude people with negative total or disposable income; the Danish sample also excludes those not living in Denmark in 1987, replicating the population represented by the SOI-M Panel.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. Types are defined by circumstances that are fixed or predetermined (gender and the fiftile of average parental disposable income when the person was 15-23 years old); inequality of opportunity is the inequality of the within-type mean incomes of people aged 35-38 in 2010, computed nonparametrically.

key_assumptions.assumption: Circumstances are only partially observed - types are defined by gender and parental income fiftile alone - so the computed AIOpI(W) is a lower bound for true AIOpI.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Analytical argument in the section on identification assumptions and the two-circumstance model of partial-observability bias (equations 1-7); stated in the notes to Tables 5-8.

key_assumptions.assumption: Annual income measured at ages 35-38 proxies long-run income without lifecycle bias: in the nonclassical measurement-error model Z = pi0*Y^pi1 + V with E(V|c)=0 for all c, pi1 is approximately 1 close to age 40, so D(E(Z|C)) = D(E(Y|C)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Evidence from Mitnik (2020b) using PSID family-income data: pi1 is approximately 1 close to age 40, E(V|c) is close to zero, and AIOpI computed with short-run income around age 40 is very close to AIOpI computed with long-run income.

formal.as_written: Z = pi0 Y^pi1 + V ; E(V|c) = 0 for all c

key_assumptions.assumption: The Danish and U.S. estimates are comparable: same birth cohorts, same ages and year, same circumstances defining types, same estimation method, aligned income notions, CPI deflators and a PPP exchange rate of 758.6 kroner per 100 dollars.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Description of the data and variables and the note to Table 4; the Danish sample replicates the SOI-M Panel's approach to assigning parents and defining families and its represented population.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on data availability and on positive parental income: people with more than 3 years of missing parental information or nonpositive average parental income are excluded, income analyses also exclude negative total or disposable income, and the Danish sample excludes those not living in the country in 1987.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated inclusion rules in the data section; no balance or sensitivity analysis of these exclusions is reported.

threats_discussed: Circumstances are only partially observed (only gender and parental income rank are used to define types), so every AIOpI and RIOpI estimate is a lower bound
Lifecycle bias from proxying long-run income with an annual income measure obtained at ages 35-38
The U.S. measure of disposable income excludes state taxes and some transfers (addressed by ex-post adjustment factors in Table 6)
The U.S. estimates come from a sample (the SOI-M Panel) with imputed income and marital status for nonfilers, whereas the Danish estimates come from full-population register data
Cross-country comparability of income concepts, deflators and the PPP conversion of Danish kroner
robustness_checks: Five inequality indices (Gini, Kakwani, Piesch, Mehran and the relative mean deviation) used for the AIOpI ratios (Figure 6)
Ex-post adjustment of the U.S. disposable-income estimates for state taxes and omitted transfers (Table 6)
Extension accounting for race and ethnicity in the U.S. with Chetty et al. (2020b) data (Table 8, Figure 8)
Estimates reported for men and women separately as well as pooled (Tables 5 and 7)
unresolved_confounders: Circumstances beyond people's control that are not observed - the paper names parental education and place of residence when growing up, and race and ethnicity in the main analyses
Which institutional factors generate the cross-country difference (labour-market institutions, early education and job training, employment structure) is left to future research

estimator.value: Nonparametric (Checchi-Peragine) estimation of inequality of opportunity: each person is assigned the mean income of their type and the Gini coefficient is computed over the resulting distribution; inference by nonparametric bootstrap with 2,000 repetitions.

estimation.specification: AIOpI(W) over 100 types (gender x fiftile of parental disposable income), full population

ambiguities: The paper is descriptive and partially identified: the circumstances-income quantity is estimated nonparametrically, not with a design that identifies a causal effect. The edge is recorded as causal_tested because the paper estimates and reports that pair, but the authors frame circumstances as predetermined rather than manipulated.
The note to Table 5 does not state the confidence level of the reported intervals.
relationship.statistically_significant is left null: the paper reports no test of this level estimate against zero.

the ex-ante Van de gaer (1993) approach to valuing opportunity sets by the mean income of people with the same circumstances

definition.value: Whether the population analysed is that of the United States (SOI-M Panel, IRS administrative data) or of Denmark (administrative register data covering the full population), with cohorts, ages, year, type definition and estimation method held fixed.

timing.value: Both countries observed in 2010, at ages 35-38.

outcome.label: Lower-bound absolute inequality of opportunity (AIOpI) for individual earnings, four inequality indices other than the Gini (Kakwani, Piesch, Mehran, relative mean deviation)

definition.value: The four inequality indices other than the Gini (Kakwani, Piesch, Mehran, relative mean deviation) computed over the distribution in which every person is assigned the mean individual earnings of their type (types = gender x parental disposable income fiftile). Because circumstances are only partially observed it is a lower bound for true AIOpI.

timing.value: Computed from incomes measured in 2010 at ages 35-38.

units.value: percent by which lower-bound AIOpI in the United States exceeds that in Denmark, averaged over the four non-Gini indices

magnitude.interpretation: The corresponding Gini-based figures are 37, 47, 55, 49 and 68 percent for earnings, total income, disposable income, total income per adult and disposable income per adult, so the comparison is very robust to the inequality index.

estimand.target_population: People born 1972-1975, aged 35-38 in 2010, in the United States and Denmark (men and women pooled)
estimand.formal_query: AIOpI_US(W) / AIOpI_DK(W), a lower bound for AIOpI_US / AIOpI_DK under IALB

population.description: People born 1972-1975 who were 35-38 years old in 2010 in Denmark and the United States. Denmark: administrative register data covering the full population; United States: the SOI-M Panel, which represents all people born 1972-1975 living in the U.S. in 1987.
population.period: 2010 (own income); parental income averaged over the years in which the person was 15-23 years old
subgroups_defined: gender
fiftiles of average parental disposable income
race and ethnicity (U.S. extension only, via Chetty et al. 2020b aggregates)
population.selection: Excludes people with more than 3 years of missing parental information and with nonpositive average parental income; income analyses also exclude people with negative total or disposable income; the Danish sample also excludes those not living in Denmark in 1987, replicating the population represented by the SOI-M Panel.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. Types are defined by circumstances that are fixed or predetermined (gender and the fiftile of average parental disposable income when the person was 15-23 years old); inequality of opportunity is the inequality of the within-type mean incomes of people aged 35-38 in 2010, computed nonparametrically. Identification of the ratio as a lower bound relies on IALB alone.

key_assumptions.assumption: Circumstances are only partially observed - types are defined by gender and parental income fiftile alone - so the computed AIOpI(W) is a lower bound for true AIOpI.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Analytical argument in the section on identification assumptions and the two-circumstance model of partial-observability bias (equations 1-7); stated in the notes to Tables 5-8.

key_assumptions.assumption: Annual income measured at ages 35-38 proxies long-run income without lifecycle bias: in the nonclassical measurement-error model Z = pi0*Y^pi1 + V with E(V|c)=0 for all c, pi1 is approximately 1 close to age 40, so D(E(Z|C)) = D(E(Y|C)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Evidence from Mitnik (2020b) using PSID family-income data: pi1 is approximately 1 close to age 40, E(V|c) is close to zero, and AIOpI computed with short-run income around age 40 is very close to AIOpI computed with long-run income.

formal.as_written: Z = pi0 Y^pi1 + V ; E(V|c) = 0 for all c

key_assumptions.assumption: The Danish and U.S. estimates are comparable: same birth cohorts, same ages and year, same circumstances defining types, same estimation method, aligned income notions, CPI deflators and a PPP exchange rate of 758.6 kroner per 100 dollars.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Description of the data and variables and the note to Table 4; the Danish sample replicates the SOI-M Panel's approach to assigning parents and defining families and its represented population.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on data availability and on positive parental income: people with more than 3 years of missing parental information or nonpositive average parental income are excluded, income analyses also exclude negative total or disposable income, and the Danish sample excludes those not living in the country in 1987.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated inclusion rules in the data section; no balance or sensitivity analysis of these exclusions is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Inequality assumption for the lower bound (IALB): the difference between AIOpI and AIOpI(W) in the United States is not smaller than the difference between AIOpI and AIOpI(W) in Denmark.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The two-circumstance model of partial-observability bias and the section 'The case for the applicability of IALB and IAUB to the comparison between the U.S. and Denmark'; no direct test is possible.

formal.as_written: AIOpI_A - AIOpI_A(W) >= AIOpI_B - AIOpI_B(W)

key_assumptions.assumption: Estimates of overall income inequality are divided by a lifecycle-bias adjustment factor computed from the PSID (1.11 for the Gini; 1.22 Kakwani, 1.12 Piesch, 1.10 Mehran, 1.11 RMD), which is assumed to transfer from the PSID to the Danish and U.S. samples.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Captions to Figures 5 and 6: a Gini for family income at ages 35-38 divided by a Gini for average income at ages 24-56, computed with 'Sample I' from Mitnik (2019).

key_assumptions.assumption: AIOp estimated with the SOI-M measure of disposable income overstates AIOp in true disposable income by the same proportional factor by which the estimation of overall inequality with that measure overstates overall inequality in true disposable income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Adjustment factors computed with CPS-ASEC data on state taxes and omitted transfers (note to Table 6); the proportionality itself is not tested.

threats_discussed: Circumstances are only partially observed (only gender and parental income rank are used to define types), so every AIOpI and RIOpI estimate is a lower bound
Lifecycle bias from proxying long-run income with an annual income measure obtained at ages 35-38
The U.S. measure of disposable income excludes state taxes and some transfers (addressed by ex-post adjustment factors in Table 6)
The U.S. estimates come from a sample (the SOI-M Panel) with imputed income and marital status for nonfilers, whereas the Danish estimates come from full-population register data
Cross-country comparability of income concepts, deflators and the PPP conversion of Danish kroner
robustness_checks: Five inequality indices (Gini, Kakwani, Piesch, Mehran and the relative mean deviation) used for the AIOpI ratios (Figure 6)
Ex-post adjustment of the U.S. disposable-income estimates for state taxes and omitted transfers (Table 6)
Extension accounting for race and ethnicity in the U.S. with Chetty et al. (2020b) data (Table 8, Figure 8)
Estimates reported for men and women separately as well as pooled (Tables 5 and 7)
unresolved_confounders: Circumstances beyond people's control that are not observed - the paper names parental education and place of residence when growing up, and race and ethnicity in the main analyses
Which institutional factors generate the cross-country difference (labour-market institutions, early education and job training, employment structure) is left to future research

estimator.value: Nonparametric (Checchi-Peragine) estimation of inequality of opportunity: each person is assigned the mean income of their type and four inequality indices (Kakwani, Piesch, Mehran, relative mean deviation) is computed over the resulting distribution; inference by nonparametric bootstrap with 2,000 repetitions.

estimation.specification: Lower-bound AIOpI ratios under IALB, averaged by the extractor-visible text across the four non-Gini indices; overall inequality corrected for lifecycle bias (factors 1.22 Kakwani, 1.12 Piesch, 1.10 Mehran, 1.11 RMD)
estimation.weights: SOI-M Panel sampling weights for the U.S. estimates; no weights mentioned for the Danish register data

sample_n.value: Denmark 263,254 and United States 13,107 (earnings-analysis samples, Table 4)

source_table.value: Figure 6 (five inequality indices, full population)

mediators_claimed: Denmark's labor-market institutions compress the earnings distribution much more than their U.S. counterparts do
Denmark invests much more heavily in early education and job training and has more generous and more expansive public-insurance programs
The two countries' welfare regimes produce employment structures with different job mixes, the U.S. one including a much larger share of low-skill personal-service jobs
ambiguities: The paper is descriptive and partially identified: the circumstances-income quantity is estimated nonparametrically, not with a design that identifies a causal effect. The edge is recorded as causal_tested because the paper estimates and reports that pair, but the authors frame circumstances as predetermined rather than manipulated.
The figure reported is the paper's own average of the four non-Gini index-specific lower-bound ratios; the index-specific values themselves are only plotted in Figure 6 and are not printed.
ci_level 95 is taken from the Figure 6 caption; it applies to the index-specific estimates plotted, not necessarily to their average.

evidence.annotation: Estimation relies on IALB, the inequality assumption for the lower bound, so estimates of overall income inequality are used as inputs for generating the lower-bound estimates of AIOpI ratios

theory_referenced: luck egalitarianism (Dworkin 1981a, 1981b; Arneson 1989; Cohen 1989; Roemer 1998)
the ex-ante Van de gaer (1993) approach to valuing opportunity sets by the mean income of people with the same circumstances
outcomes_examined_not_reported: AIOpI estimates with the generalized-entropy index with sensitivity parameter 2: computed but 'very imprecise' and not reported (footnote 46)

treatment.label: Fiftile of average parental disposable income

definition.value: Rank of the person's parents in 50 equally sized groups (2 percent each) of average parental disposable family income, measured when the person was 15-23 years old.

timing.value: Parental disposable income averaged over the years in which the person was 15-23 years old.

outcome.label: Total family income

definition.value: Pre-tax-and-transfer family income in 2010. Denmark: the sum of labour earnings (including 100 percent of self-employment income), capital income and unemployment insurance. All income variables are expressed in 2010 U.S. dollars (CPI deflators; Danish kroner converted at a PPP rate of 758.6 kroner per 100 dollars).

timing.value: Measured in 2010, when the people in the sample were 35-38 years old; the quantity of interest is long-run income, for which the 2010 measure is a proxy.

units.value: 2010 U.S. dollars of mean total family income per one-fiftile increase in parental disposable income

magnitude.interpretation: The average slope of the opportunity curve across the 50 parental income fiftiles, computed from within-type mean income values; the paper states it as an approximation ('about' / 'close to' / 'as much as').

population.description: People born 1972-1975 who were 35-38 years old in 2010 in the United States, women only. The SOI-M Panel, which represents all people born 1972-1975 who were living in the U.S. in 1987.

subgroups_defined: gender
fiftiles of average parental disposable income
race and ethnicity (U.S. extension only, via Chetty et al. 2020b aggregates)
population.selection: Excludes people with more than 3 years of missing parental information and with nonpositive average parental income; income analyses also exclude people with negative total or disposable income; the Danish sample also excludes those not living in Denmark in 1987, replicating the population represented by the SOI-M Panel.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. Types are defined by circumstances that are fixed or predetermined (gender and the fiftile of average parental disposable income when the person was 15-23 years old); inequality of opportunity is the inequality of the within-type mean incomes of people aged 35-38 in 2010, computed nonparametrically.

key_assumptions.assumption: Circumstances are only partially observed - types are defined by gender and parental income fiftile alone - so the computed AIOpI(W) is a lower bound for true AIOpI.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Analytical argument in the section on identification assumptions and the two-circumstance model of partial-observability bias (equations 1-7); stated in the notes to Tables 5-8.

key_assumptions.assumption: Annual income measured at ages 35-38 proxies long-run income without lifecycle bias: in the nonclassical measurement-error model Z = pi0*Y^pi1 + V with E(V|c)=0 for all c, pi1 is approximately 1 close to age 40, so D(E(Z|C)) = D(E(Y|C)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Evidence from Mitnik (2020b) using PSID family-income data: pi1 is approximately 1 close to age 40, E(V|c) is close to zero, and AIOpI computed with short-run income around age 40 is very close to AIOpI computed with long-run income.

formal.as_written: Z = pi0 Y^pi1 + V ; E(V|c) = 0 for all c

key_assumptions.supported_by: Description of the data and variables and the note to Table 4; the Danish sample replicates the SOI-M Panel's approach to assigning parents and defining families and its represented population.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on data availability and on positive parental income: people with more than 3 years of missing parental information or nonpositive average parental income are excluded, income analyses also exclude negative total or disposable income, and the Danish sample excludes those not living in the country in 1987.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated inclusion rules in the data section; no balance or sensitivity analysis of these exclusions is reported.

threats_discussed: Circumstances are only partially observed (only gender and parental income rank are used to define types), so every AIOpI and RIOpI estimate is a lower bound

The U.S. estimates come from a sample (the SOI-M Panel) with imputed income and marital status for nonfilers, whereas the Danish estimates come from full-population register data
Cross-country comparability of income concepts, deflators and the PPP conversion of Danish kroner
robustness_checks: Five inequality indices (Gini, Kakwani, Piesch, Mehran and the relative mean deviation) used for the AIOpI ratios (Figure 6)
Ex-post adjustment of the U.S. disposable-income estimates for state taxes and omitted transfers (Table 6)
Extension accounting for race and ethnicity in the U.S. with Chetty et al. (2020b) data (Table 8, Figure 8)
Estimates reported for men and women separately as well as pooled (Tables 5 and 7)

unresolved_confounders: Circumstances beyond people's control that are not observed - the paper names parental education and place of residence when growing up, and race and ethnicity in the main analyses

the ex-ante Van de gaer (1993) approach to valuing opportunity sets by the mean income of people with the same circumstances

claims.statement: The MLD-based lower-bound absolute inequality of opportunity for men's individual earnings is as much as seven times larger in the United States than in Denmark.

treatment.label: Country: the United States versus Denmark

definition.value: Whether the population analysed is that of the United States (SOI-M Panel, IRS administrative data) or of Denmark (administrative register data covering the full population), with cohorts, ages, year, type definition and estimation method held fixed.

timing.value: Both countries observed in 2010, at ages 35-38.

outcome.label: Lower-bound absolute inequality of opportunity (AIOpI) for individual earnings, mean logarithmic deviation

definition.value: The mean logarithmic deviation computed over the distribution in which every person is assigned the mean individual earnings of their type (types = gender x parental disposable income fiftile). Because circumstances are only partially observed it is a lower bound for true AIOpI.

timing.value: Computed from incomes measured in 2010 at ages 35-38.

units.value: ratio of the MLD-based lower-bound AIOp for men's earnings in the United States to that in Denmark

magnitude.interpretation: Table 5 gives MLD-based AIOp for men's earnings of 0.100 in the United States and 0.014 in Denmark; for men and women pooled, and for women alone, the paper says the U.S. value is between four and five times larger.

estimand.target_population: Men born 1972-1975, aged 35-38 in 2010, in the United States and Denmark
estimand.formal_query: MLD(E(Y|C))_US / MLD(E(Y|C))_DK for men's individual earnings

population.description: People born 1972-1975 who were 35-38 years old in 2010 in Denmark and the United States, men only. Denmark: administrative register data covering the full population; United States: the SOI-M Panel, which represents all people born 1972-1975 living in the U.S. in 1987.
population.period: 2010 (own income); parental income averaged over the years in which the person was 15-23 years old
subgroups_defined: gender
fiftiles of average parental disposable income
race and ethnicity (U.S. extension only, via Chetty et al. 2020b aggregates)
population.selection: Excludes people with more than 3 years of missing parental information and with nonpositive average parental income; income analyses also exclude people with negative total or disposable income; the Danish sample also excludes those not living in Denmark in 1987, replicating the population represented by the SOI-M Panel.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used. Types are defined by circumstances that are fixed or predetermined (gender and the fiftile of average parental disposable income when the person was 15-23 years old); inequality of opportunity is the inequality of the within-type mean incomes of people aged 35-38 in 2010, computed nonparametrically.

key_assumptions.assumption: Circumstances are only partially observed - types are defined by gender and parental income fiftile alone - so the computed AIOpI(W) is a lower bound for true AIOpI.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Analytical argument in the section on identification assumptions and the two-circumstance model of partial-observability bias (equations 1-7); stated in the notes to Tables 5-8.

key_assumptions.assumption: Annual income measured at ages 35-38 proxies long-run income without lifecycle bias: in the nonclassical measurement-error model Z = pi0*Y^pi1 + V with E(V|c)=0 for all c, pi1 is approximately 1 close to age 40, so D(E(Z|C)) = D(E(Y|C)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Evidence from Mitnik (2020b) using PSID family-income data: pi1 is approximately 1 close to age 40, E(V|c) is close to zero, and AIOpI computed with short-run income around age 40 is very close to AIOpI computed with long-run income.

formal.as_written: Z = pi0 Y^pi1 + V ; E(V|c) = 0 for all c

key_assumptions.assumption: The Danish and U.S. estimates are comparable: same birth cohorts, same ages and year, same circumstances defining types, same estimation method, aligned income notions, CPI deflators and a PPP exchange rate of 758.6 kroner per 100 dollars.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Description of the data and variables and the note to Table 4; the Danish sample replicates the SOI-M Panel's approach to assigning parents and defining families and its represented population.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on data availability and on positive parental income: people with more than 3 years of missing parental information or nonpositive average parental income are excluded, income analyses also exclude negative total or disposable income, and the Danish sample excludes those not living in the country in 1987.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated inclusion rules in the data section; no balance or sensitivity analysis of these exclusions is reported.

threats_discussed: Circumstances are only partially observed (only gender and parental income rank are used to define types), so every AIOpI and RIOpI estimate is a lower bound
Lifecycle bias from proxying long-run income with an annual income measure obtained at ages 35-38
The U.S. measure of disposable income excludes state taxes and some transfers (addressed by ex-post adjustment factors in Table 6)
The U.S. estimates come from a sample (the SOI-M Panel) with imputed income and marital status for nonfilers, whereas the Danish estimates come from full-population register data
Cross-country comparability of income concepts, deflators and the PPP conversion of Danish kroner
robustness_checks: Five inequality indices (Gini, Kakwani, Piesch, Mehran and the relative mean deviation) used for the AIOpI ratios (Figure 6)
Ex-post adjustment of the U.S. disposable-income estimates for state taxes and omitted transfers (Table 6)
Extension accounting for race and ethnicity in the U.S. with Chetty et al. (2020b) data (Table 8, Figure 8)
Estimates reported for men and women separately as well as pooled (Tables 5 and 7)
unresolved_confounders: Circumstances beyond people's control that are not observed - the paper names parental education and place of residence when growing up, and race and ethnicity in the main analyses
Which institutional factors generate the cross-country difference (labour-market institutions, early education and job training, employment structure) is left to future research

estimator.value: Nonparametric (Checchi-Peragine) estimation of inequality of opportunity: each person is assigned the mean income of their type and the mean logarithmic deviation is computed over the resulting distribution; inference by nonparametric bootstrap with 2,000 repetitions.

estimation.specification: Ratio of the MLD-based lower-bound AIOp for men's earnings in the two countries (50 types defined by parental income fiftile)
estimation.weights: SOI-M Panel sampling weights for the U.S. estimates; no weights mentioned for the Danish register data

sample_n.value: Denmark 263,254 and United States 13,107 (earnings-analysis samples, Table 4)

source_table.value: Text, page 29, drawing on Table 5, panel 'Men', MLD columns

nodes: effort and other determinants of income

ambiguities: The paper is descriptive and partially identified: the circumstances-income quantity is estimated nonparametrically, not with a design that identifies a causal effect. The edge is recorded as causal_tested because the paper estimates and reports that pair, but the authors frame circumstances as predetermined rather than manipulated.
The paper words this as 'as much as seven times larger'; the ratio of the Table 5 values (0.100 / 0.014) is about 7.1. The value 7 recorded here is the paper's own wording, not a printed ratio.
This ratio of lower bounds is not itself presented as a bound on the true AIOp ratio; the set estimates under IALB and IAUB (Figure 5) serve that purpose and are Gini-based.
